title: Blues slide from the #9 into the 3rd

review.reviewedBy: Claude, the AI that wrote it

inspiration.note: Wes often mixed blue notes into his ii–V lines, such as the minor-3rd blue note over the dominant chord, and slid into target notes from a fret below; this phrase uses both habits.

sources.title: The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery
sources.author: Wes Montgomery
sources.detail: Riverside, recorded January 1960; includes his own blues 'D-Natural Blues' and 'West Coast Blues'.

sources.title: 40 Wes Montgomery Jazz Guitar Licks, Patterns, Chords & Solos
sources.author: Dirk Laukens
sources.detail: JazzGuitar.be: blue notes mixed into ii–V–I lines, including the b3 blue note (G#/Ab) over F7, the minor pentatonic of the ii over the V, and approaching notes chromatically by sliding into them.

analysis.summary: Over {{chord 1}} the line stays inside the minor pentatonic scale, with a little bluesy turn around the 5th. That 5th then rises chromatically: {{note 2.1}}, the #9 of {{chord 2}}, slides up a half step into {{note 2.2}}, its 3rd, the classic blues move from a minor-3rd sound to a major 3rd. The b7 and a chromatic note from below then frame the 3rd of {{chord 3}}, which lands on beat one.

points.text: The pentatonic notes in bar 1 are strong notes of {{chord 1}}: b7, root and 5th. In bar 2, {{note 2.2}}, {{note 2.3}} and {{note 2.4}} are the 3rd, 5th and b7 of {{chord 2}}, and bar 3 lands on the 3rd of {{chord 3}} and finishes on its root.

{{note 2.1}} is the #9 of {{chord 2}}. It sounds like a minor 3rd, the blue note, rubbing against the major 3rd of the chord. Sliding it up into {{note 2.2}} turns that rub into the blues-inspired sound heard in many Wes Montgomery solos.

{{note 1.6}} is a lower neighbour that dips under the 5th and comes straight back. {{note 2.6}} approaches the 3rd of {{chord 3}} from a half step below, and with {{note 2.4}} a half step above, the target is framed from both sides. {{note 3.2}} passes between the 3rd and the root at the end.

The phrase starts on the 'and' of one. The slide is timed so the #9 hits the downbeat of bar 2 and the 3rd arrives on the 'and'. The rest on beat four of bar 2 is a short breath before the pickup into {{chord 3}}; rests like this make a line sound spoken rather than run.
{{note 3.1}} is the 3rd of {{chord 3}}, reached from a half step below on beat one. After the blues colour of the first two bars, a plain chord tone on the downbeat makes the arrival sound settled.

whyItWorks: Over {{chord 1}}, the minor pentatonic scale built on its root sounds bluesy with no clashing notes. On {{chord 2}} the #9 is the blues' minor 3rd: sliding it up into the major 3rd gives the ear a moment of grit and then the right note, which is what makes blues phrasing sound vocal.
fingeringNote: Eighth position: index finger on fret 8, little finger on fret 11; bar 1 sits in the minor pentatonic box here. For the slide in bar 2, put the middle finger on fret 9 of the B string, pick once and slide it up to fret 10 while the rest of the hand stays put; the index finger is then ready for fret 8 on the high E string.
practiceTask: Play the lick over bars 9 to 11 of the weekly standard, then over bars 1 to 3 and 21 to 23, which use the same chords. Practise the slide on its own first: pick the #9 exactly on the beat and arrive on the 3rd exactly on the 'and'.

variation.description: Slide into the landing as well: {{note 1.6}} now slides up a half step into {{note 2.1}}, the 3rd of {{chord 2}}, just as the #9 slid into the 3rd of {{chord 1}}. Use the middle finger for both slides, and both arrivals sound sung rather than picked. Only these last two bars change; play the first bar as written.
